messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Questions about maps & stratification
parts:
Hi Fernando, list,

Can't answer your first question I'm afraid, not being a GIS guy. But as to
your second:

> >2. We do boat-based line surveys for marine mammals in a relatively small
> >area, divided in two strata: inshore and offshore. We did 48 transect legs
> >during the summer and have analysed the data using DISTANCE. We got very
> >large values for %CV and 95%CI. Our problem, I guess, is that our sample
> >sizes are very modest (23 observations of bottlenose dolphins, 45 of harbour
> >porpoise and 25 of grey seals). We have additional data taken from the same
> >platform and under similar conditions, but collected while not following
> >strict transect protocol (i.e.: while in transit to waypoints or during
> >whale-watching trips). Could we use this additional data as if belonging to
> >a third stratum, and ask DISTANCE to estimate the detection function
> >globally and the density per strata only? The sample size would be greatly
> >increased this way. Would this help to reduce the CV & CI? Is this legal? If
> >so, how do we handle the CV & CI when we want to add up the values on the
> >two important strata (inshore and offshore) in order to produce estimates of
> >abundance in the whole area?

Firstly, you should check what's causing the large CV. Remember that there are
three components of estimation: detection function, encounter rate and expected
cluster size. All contribute to the overall variance. You can see the
percentage contributions in the Analysis Details | Results, at the bottom of the
page with the title that starts "Density Estimates". If there is only a small
percentage due to estimating the detection function then the procedure you
describe won't help much in reducing the CV.

Secondly, to decide whether it's "legal" or not, think about whether you're
violating any of the assumptions of the method. Normally, our transect lines
are placed at random (or random systematic, etc), so that the density of animals
is uniform with respect to distance from the transect. In your case for the
non-random effort, is there any reason to think that the density of animals will
not be uniform within the strips? For example, are many of the non-random
transects parallel to the shore and close in, with density of animals increasing
rapidly as you go away from the shore, etc etc. Also, are there any other
reasons to suspect a different detection function in these transects vs the
others (e.g., observers not paying so much attention, etc). If not, then I
don't see a problem in combining them to estimate the detection function -- but
with so few data you're not going to be able to test the assumption that the
observations from the non-random surveys are compatible, so it's a leap of
faith.

Even if including the other observations isn't going to decrease the CV much,
you may want to do it to increase the sample size -- 23 is really getting pretty
small to be fitting a detection function to - even if the observation process
has a wide shoulder, etc...

One way to do what you want in Distance is to use the multipliers facility.
You'd fit a detection function to all the data and write down the estimated p
and SE p. Type these in as multipliers and then do a second analysis using only
the strata you're interested in, fitting a uniform detection function with no
adjustments (effectively a strip transect) but dividing the density estimates by
the multiplier p. This is documented in the online manual -- look in the index
under Multipliers and look at the bottom bit of the page where it says
Additional Uses of Multipliers.

You could also do it using stratification as you suggest, but then you'll have
to work out the variance of abundance for the whole area (when you add the two
important strata together) by hand using the formulae in Introduction to
Distance Sampling (see the section on stratification there for an example).

Cheers,

- Len
